patches.old: Combined with \cref{eq:paper-spurious-floor-even-odd}, $E_n(a)^*=E_n(a)$: the eigenvalues of the PT-odd class are \emph{exactly real} for every amplitude below the first collision. patches.new:
Combined with \cref{eq:paper-spurious-floor-even-odd}, $E_n(a)^*=E_n(a)$: for small enough $|a|$ the eigenvalues of the PT-odd class are \emph{exactly real}.

The reality persists to larger amplitudes, up to the first collision, by a continuation argument. Take any real $a$. If $E$ is an eigenvalue of $H(a)$, then $E^*$ is an eigenvalue of $H(-a)$ (conjugation, \cref{eq:paper-spurious-floor-conj}). Also $H(-a)$ has the same eigenvalues as $H(a)$ (similarity, just shown). So the spectrum of $H(a)$ is closed under complex conjugation: non-real eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs $E,E^*$.

Now follow a simple real eigenvalue as $a$ grows; it moves continuously. Suppose it first leaves the real axis at an amplitude $a_*$, at the real point $E_*$. Just beyond $a_*$ it is a non-real $E$ close to $E_*$, and its partner $E^*$ is a distinct eigenvalue, also close to $E_*$. As $a\to a_*$ both tend to $E_*$, so at $a_*$ two eigenvalues coincide: a collision. A real eigenvalue can therefore become complex only at a collision. Hence the PT-odd spectrum stays exactly real for every amplitude below the first collision on the real $a$-axis. Beyond it, eigenvalues may pair off into complex conjugates (PT symmetry breaking, Chapter~\ref{ch:non-hermitian}).

patches.new: The update is Levenberg--Marquardt with ``diag scaling'' (Marquardt's form, Chapter~\ref{ch:fitting}): solve $(J^\top J+\lambda\,\mathrm{diag}(J^\top J))\,\delta c=-J^\top r$, trying damping values $(0.3\lambda,\lambda,10\lambda)$. Plain damping adds $\lambda$ times the identity matrix. Replacing the identity by $\mathrm{diag}(J^\top J)$ damps each coefficient in proportion to its own sensitivity, so the step does not change if one coefficient is rescaled (say, measured in different units). patches.old: Once $(\phi_0)_{nm}=\eta_{nm}\ne0$ off the diagonal, the operator matrix becomes $A_{nm}=c_0\eta_{nm}+\sum_{l\ge1}c_l(\phi_l)_{nm}$. The constant mode now contributes a \emph{pseudo-random matrix} $c_0\eta_{nm}$. With entries $\eta\sim10^{-9}$ to $10^{-7}$, a coefficient $c_0=2.2\times10^6$ makes $c_0\eta$ of order $2.2\times10^{-3}$ to $0.26$ in energy units, comparable with level spacings of order 1. A random matrix of the right size is a new, arbitrary set of features, and an unconstrained least-squares fit will use any feature that reduces the residual, however meaningless.
patches.new:
What follows is one possible route by which such noise can act, and the reconstruction is ours. The paper says only that the noise sat in the stored float32 tensor entries $T^{(n)}_{0l}$. That noise may have arisen from rounding of the overlaps, of the state sums, or of both. Suppose, for illustration, that the overlaps carry noise, $(\phi_0)_{nm}=\eta_{nm}\ne0$ off the diagonal. Then the operator matrix becomes $A_{nm}=c_0\eta_{nm}+\sum_{l\ge1}c_l(\phi_l)_{nm}$, and the constant mode contributes a \emph{pseudo-random matrix} $c_0\eta_{nm}$. Take entries $\eta$ of size $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-7}$ (an assumed range covering float32 rounding levels). A coefficient $c_0=2.2\times10^6$ then makes $c_0\eta$ of order $2\times10^{-3}$ to $0.2$ in energy units, up to a sizeable fraction of a level spacing (spacings here are of order 1).

Whatever the route, the effect on the fit is the same. The tensor rows $T^{(n)}_{0l}$ stop being zero, and $c_0$ multiplies a set of meaningless, pseudo-random numbers. Such numbers form a new, arbitrary set of features, and an unconstrained least-squares fit will use any feature that reduces the residual, however meaningless.

        A += c*(-1)**j/2*((abs(kk-ll)==2*j).astype(float)-(kk+ll==2*j).astype(float))
    return k**2.0, A
